planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines or containerized plants in early spring once the soil is workable, in a spot with full sun and long, hot summers.

directions: Set vines against a sturdy trellis or arbor in deep, well-drained soil, spacing plants widely to allow for vigorous cane growth, and prune hard each dormant season to renew fruiting wood. This old California cultivar, also known as Sultanina, produces small, oval, amber-green berries in loose to medium clusters with no seeds and thin, sweet skin. It is the classic grape dried into raisins and is equally popular fresh, but it needs a long, hot growing season to ripen and size up well. Vines are vigorous and productive but more cold-tender than American-type grapes, so winter protection is worthwhile at the cooler edge of its range.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or containerized vines in early spring against a trellis or arbor in full sun.

directions: Train young vines onto a permanent support system and prune annually in dormancy, since fruit forms on the current season's growth from one-year-old canes. Crimson Seedless bears elongated, crisp, pink-to-red berries with a mild, sweet flavor on large, well-filled clusters that ripen late in the season. It is a late-season companion to earlier seedless grapes, extending the fresh-eating harvest into fall, and tends to color best where nights cool down as the fruit matures. Like most vinifera grapes it prefers a long, warm growing season and struggles in areas with high humidity and fungal disease pressure.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in early spring once the ground can be worked, siting them along a fence or trellis in full sun.

directions: Grow this cold-hardy American grape on a two- or four-arm kniffin trellis, pruning heavily each winter to keep fruiting wood renewed and clusters well spaced. It produces the same deep blue-black, musky-sweet slip-skin berries prized in classic Concord grape juice and jelly, but without the seeds that fill traditional Concord fruit, making it far more pleasant for fresh eating. The vines share Concord's toughness and reliable heavy cropping in short-season northern climates, though clusters are typically a bit smaller and looser than the seeded parent. It is self-fruitful and widely adapted to home gardens outside hot, humid grape-growing regions.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root bushes in early spring into acidic, well-drained, organic-rich soil.

directions: Site bushes in full sun on acidic soil amended with peat or pine bark and mulch heavily to keep shallow roots cool and moist. Chandler is famous for producing some of the largest berries of any highbush blueberry, often nickel- to quarter-sized, with a mild, sweet flavor and a very long harvest window since ripe fruit holds well on the bush. Its extended ripening period spreads picking over several weeks rather than concentrating it into a short flush. Vigorous, upright canes benefit from a second pollinator variety nearby to improve fruit set and size.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root bushes in early spring into acidic, moisture-retentive soil.

directions: Grow in full sun on well-drained, acidic soil and mulch with pine bark or sawdust to hold moisture around the shallow, fibrous root system. Berkeley is an older, widely planted mid-season highbush cultivar valued for large, firm, pale sky-blue berries with a mild, sweet flavor and good resistance to cracking. Its spreading, vigorous bushes are heavy and reliable producers over a long lifespan, and the plant also offers attractive orange-red fall foliage. Because it dislikes waterlogged soil, raised beds or amended rows are worthwhile on heavier ground.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring into fast-draining, mineral-rich, acidic soil in an open, sunny site.

directions: Grow this low, wiry-branched shrub in gritty, well-drained, acidic soil that mimics its native volcanic cinder habitat, and avoid rich garden soil or heavy watering that can encourage rot. Ohelo produces small, tart-sweet, cranberry-like berries in shades of red, yellow, or orange, borne alongside dainty urn-shaped pink or yellow flowers typical of the blueberry family. Native to high-elevation Hawaiian volcanic slopes, it tolerates poor, rocky ground and strong sun but is sensitive to wet, poorly drained conditions and to frost. The tangy fruit is traditionally used fresh or cooked into jams and sauces.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources

planting.note: Plant dormant crowns or rooted tip cuttings in early spring along a trellis in full sun.

directions: Train the long, trailing canes onto a wire trellis and thin out spent floricanes after harvest to keep the planting productive and easy to pick. Kotata is a vigorous trailing blackberry developed for the Pacific Northwest that produces large, firm, glossy black berries with a rich, tart-sweet flavor well suited to both fresh eating and processing into jams and baked goods. It ripens in mid-summer with good yields on second-year canes and holds up well to shipping compared to older trailing types. The canes carry thorns, so gloves and careful trellis training make harvest and maintenance easier.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil and stake young trees for their first year or two, since they establish quickly and grow at a moderate to fast rate. Canada Red is a selection of the native chokecherry whose new leaves emerge green in spring and gradually deepen to a rich burgundy-purple by summer, providing strong seasonal color alongside white spring flower clusters. It bears heavy clusters of small, tart, dark red-to-black cherries that are astringent fresh but make excellent jelly, syrup, and wine once cooked with sugar. Extremely cold-hardy and adaptable, it is a popular multi-purpose shelterbelt and specimen tree across the northern Plains and prairie provinces.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in early spring into moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant in fertile, evenly moist soil and prune out the oldest stems each dormant season to keep the multi-stemmed shrub productive, since fruit forms on both new and one-year-old wood. Haschberg is a European black elderberry selection widely grown across Central Europe for its heavy clusters of small, dark purple-black berries used in juice, syrup, and wine production. It produces broad, flat flower heads of creamy white blooms in early summer that are themselves used for cordials, followed by large, drooping fruit clusters in late summer. It is vigorous and consistently productive, and benefits from a second elderberry cultivar nearby for improved pollination and yield.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in early spring in average to moist soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant in average garden soil that stays reliably moist and prune out a few of the oldest canes each year to keep the upright, suckering shrub full and vigorous. Brilliantissima is a selection of native red chokeberry prized for its glossy, dark green summer foliage that turns brilliant scarlet in fall, paired with clusters of small white spring flowers and abundant bright red berries that persist into winter. The astringent fruit is not usually eaten fresh but is popular for jams, syrups, and wildlife forage, since birds tend to leave it until late in the season. It tolerates wet soil, drought, and a wide range of conditions, making it a tough, low-maintenance hedge or naturalized planting choice.
